extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and museum zoologists working on freshwater sponges (Spongillidæ) and sponge taxonomy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and diagnostic characters for describing, identifying, and classifying freshwater sponges (family Spongillidæ), emphasizing skeletal/spicule morphology, external form, cell types, variation, and reproductive structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of skeleton and spicules for recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the Spongillidæ the spicules and the skeleton are more important as regards the recognition of genera and species than the soft parts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the skeleton and spicule characters as primary taxonomic features; soft parts (cells, membranes) are less reliable. Examine arrangement, types, and shapes of spicules and the overall skeleton when distinguishing genera and species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeletal architecture (reticulate vs. mass; radiating and transverse fibres)
rubrics_metrics.description: The skeleton is usually reticulate, but sometimes consists of a mass of spicules almost without arrangement. Reticulate skeletons form fibres of two kinds--radiating fibres and transverse fibres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record whether the skeleton is reticulate or chaotic, whether radiating fibres penetrate the external membrane, the presence/strength of transverse fibres (single spicules or splayed hour-glass forms), and how fibres are bound (spongin sheath, veil). These arrangements are diagnostic at genus/species level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Megasclere morphology (skeleton-spicules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal spicules of the skeleton are always rod-like or needle-like, and either blunt or pointed at both ends; they are either smooth, granular, or covered with small spines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe megasclere shape (needle-like, rod-like), tip form (pointed/blunt), surface texture (smooth/granular/spiny), presence of a central organic filament and any terminal protuberances. Note arrangement parallel/overlapping in fibres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscleres / free spicules (flesh-spicules) and their forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Free spicules are usually needle-like and pointed, but in a few species are of variable or irregular form, or consist of several shafts meeting in a central nodule; free microscleres may be smooth, granular, or spiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine presence/absence, shape variability (including multi-shaft or recurved-hook forms like 'double grappling-iron'), surface ornamentation, and distribution in membrane/substance. Free microscleres can be critical diagnostic characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule and gemmule-spicule characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmule-spicules... are of the greatest importance in distinguishing the genera. In simplest form they resemble free microscleres, but many bear transverse disks or rows of spines (comb-like) near ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When gemmules are mature, record presence/absence of gemmule-spicules, their shape (disked ends, indented edges, comb-like spines), and arrangement in the gemmule armature. Gemmule-spicule morphology is often genus-level diagnostic and rarely absent in mature gemmules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount and distribution of spongin
rubrics_metrics.description: The spongin that binds the skeleton-spicules together takes the form of a colourless or yellowish transparent membrane... When very abundant it sometimes extends across the nodes of the skeleton as a delicate veil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quantity and distribution of spongin (profuse sheath, veil across nodes, basal membrane, continuity with radiating fibres). Spongin abundance affects skeleton appearance and consistency and is an important character for separation of taxa (and for interpreting skeleton structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: External form and surface features (branching, lichenoid forms, oscula)
rubrics_metrics.description: The external form of sponges is very variable, but each species, subspecies, or variety of the Spongillidæ has normally a characteristic appearance. The form of the oscula is characteristic in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document gross habit (branching vs lichenoid vs cushion vs thin film vs turreted projections), surface ornamentation (ridges, conical/digitate processes, turret-like projections), and oscula morphology (size, margin definition, stellate appearance, raised cones). Use these external characters as species-typical where stable, but beware of plasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour and odour (sources and diagnostic implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most freshwater sponges have a bad odour... The coloration of freshwater sponges is usually dull and uniform; colours are due to (1) inhalation of particles, (2) pigments produced by the sponge, and (3) green corpuscles (algal). Parasitic algae may also colour dying sponges green.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record colour and odour, and attempt to distinguish causes: retained inorganic particles (washability experiment—e.g., carmine uptake and loss), intracellular pigments, presence of green corpuscles (likely algal), or parasitic algal overgrowth. Colour alone can be misleading (e.g., mud-dyed specimens or algal parasites). Odour may be characteristic but its function is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and its determinants (hardness, brittleness, softness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spongillidæ differ greatly in consistency. The consistency of a sponge depends on two factors--the number of spicules present, and the amount of spongin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note texture (stony/pumice-like, hard but brittle, soft/compressible) and relate to measurable features: spicule abundance, reticulation, and spongin amount. Compare examples (Corvospongilla lapidosa: many interlocking spicules, little spongin; Spongilla crassissima: reticulate skeleton + profuse spongin; S. carteri var. mollis: reduced spicules and spongin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic cell types and canal system (porocytes, collar-cells, ciliated chambers, bubble-cells)
rubrics_metrics.description: The walls are pierced by pores; collar-cells (choanocytes) form the gastral layer and ciliated chambers; porocytes may form pore rings or be subdermal; 'bubble-cells' are characteristic of some species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the inhalant aperture structure (porocytes vs spaces between cells), ciliated chamber arrangement, collar-cell morphology, and presence of distinctive cell types (e.g., bubble-cells). Note observation tips (porocytes difficult to see in sections—mount fragment whole). These microanatomical features have systematic importance in some genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation and phenotypic plasticity (seasonal, environmental, unexplained)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponges are very variable... Some species vary with season, others with environment, and many vary without apparent cause; spicule shape and external form can change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret morphological characters with caution: document season and habitat, and consider environmental causes (water currents, substrate, salinity, turbidity) and seasonal stage when using characters diagnostically. Examples: branching suppressed in poor conditions; oscula/ridges formed by current action; spicule tip bluntness varying seasonally. Variation may affect both individuals and whole breeds; use multiple lines of evidence (skeleton, gemmules) before erecting taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductive modes and taxonomic relevance (eggs, buds, gemmules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponges reproduce by eggs, by buds, and by gemmules; gemmules attain an elaboration of structure not observed in other families and are important in classification. Some species bud frequently and rarely reproduce sexually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record reproductive condition (presence of eggs, buds, mature gemmules) and use gemmule structure and gemmule-spicules as key diagnostic characters. Note that breeding mode (frequent budding vs sexual reproduction) may be species-specific (e.g., Spongilla proliferens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding mechanism and ecological notes (collar-cell currents, nutrition implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: All sponges obtain their food by means of the currents of water set up by the flagella of the collar-cells. The collar-cells select and engulf suitable particles; green corpuscles may contribute nutrition by photosynthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand feeding/physiology for ecological interpretation (e.g., coloration due to ingested particles or algal symbionts) but treat feeding characters as secondary for taxonomic separation. Note experiments (e.g., carmine uptake) demonstrating particle ingestion and elimination.
